explanation:
## How to Size a Water Pipe by Flow Rate

The fundamental formula is the **continuity equation**:

> **Q = V × A**

Where:
- **Q** = flow rate (m³/s)
- **V** = fluid velocity (m/s)
- **A** = pipe cross-sectional area = π × D² / 4

Rearranging to solve for diameter:

> **D = √(4Q / πV)**

This calculator uses **V = 1.5 m/s**, the value recommended by most residential plumbing standards (IAPMO, EN 806-3) to balance pressure drop, noise, and pipe wear. The result is the **minimum inner diameter**; always round up to the next commercial size.

---

## How the Calculation Works — Step by Step

1. **Convert flow rate** to m³/s if needed (1 L/s = 0.001 m³/s; 1 L/min = 0.0000167 m³/s)
2. **Choose target velocity** based on application (see table below)
3. **Apply the formula**: D = √(4 × Q / π × V)
4. **Round up** to the nearest standard commercial inner diameter
5. **Verify pressure drop** for the full pipe run — diameter alone doesn't guarantee adequate pressure at the fixture

**Worked example:** A shower requires 0.2 L/s. At 1.5 m/s:
D = √(4 × 0.0002 / π × 1.5) = √(0.000170) ≈ **0.0130 m = 13 mm inner diameter** → select 13 mm nominal pipe ✓

---

## Flow Rate → Standard Pipe Size Table

| Flow Rate (L/s) | Min. Inner Ø (mm) | Standard Pipe Size |
|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 9 mm | 13 mm |
| 0.2 | 13 mm | 13 mm |
| 0.3 | 16 mm | 20 mm |
| 0.5 | 21 mm | 25 mm |
| 0.8 | 26 mm | 32 mm |
| 1.0 | 29 mm | 32 mm |
| 1.5 | 36 mm | 40 mm |
| 2.0 | 41 mm | 50 mm |
| 3.0 | 50 mm | 50 mm |
| 5.0 | 65 mm | 75 mm |
| 8.0 | 82 mm | 90 mm |
| 10.0 | 92 mm | 110 mm |

*Standard commercial inner diameters: 13, 20, 25, 32, 40, 50, 63, 75, 90, 110 mm*

> **Note on nominal vs. inner diameter:** Pipe labels (DN/NPS) refer to nominal size, not actual inner diameter. A DN25 PVC pipe typically has an inner diameter of ~21–23 mm depending on pressure rating (SDR/PN class). Always check the manufacturer datasheet for the specific pipe series you are installing.

---

## Recommended Velocity by Application

| Application | Velocity Range | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Residential supply (cold) | 1.0 – 2.0 m/s | Above 2 m/s causes audible water hammer in residential systems |
| Residential supply (hot) | 0.5 – 1.5 m/s | Higher temps accelerate erosion; keep velocity conservative |
| Commercial / industrial | 1.5 – 3.0 m/s | Larger systems tolerate more noise; cost savings on pipe diameter |
| Fire suppression (sprinklers) | up to 5 m/s | Short-duration flow; erosion is not a long-term concern |
| Recirculation / low-pressure loops | 0.3 – 0.8 m/s | Preventing stagnation matters more than pipe size |

Higher velocity → smaller, cheaper pipe, but **greater pressure loss per meter** (proportional to V² per the Darcy-Weisbach equation). Doubling velocity roughly quadruples friction losses.

---

## Typical Fixture Flow Rates for Reference

| Fixture | Typical demand (L/s) |
|---|---|
| Kitchen faucet | 0.10 – 0.15 |
| Bathroom faucet | 0.07 – 0.10 |
| Shower | 0.15 – 0.20 |
| Bathtub fill | 0.20 – 0.30 |
| Toilet flush valve | 0.50 – 1.00 |
| Garden hose (½″) | 0.20 – 0.35 |
| Washing machine | 0.15 – 0.20 |

These values align with EN 806-3 and are useful for estimating simultaneous demand using **diversity factors** in multi-fixture systems.

---

## What This Calculator Does NOT Include

- **Pressure drop along the pipe run** — a correctly sized diameter can still deliver insufficient pressure if the pipe is long or has many fittings. Use the Hazen-Williams or Darcy-Weisbach equations for full head-loss analysis.
- **Elevation changes** — every 1 meter of height costs approximately 0.098 bar (9.8 kPa) of pressure.
- **Simultaneous demand / diversity factors** — in buildings with multiple fixtures, not all run at once. EN 806-3 and local plumbing codes provide demand unit methods to calculate realistic peak flow.
- **Water hammer / surge pressure** — relevant when solenoid valves or quick-closing fixtures are present.
- **Material-specific roughness** — smooth pipes (PEX, PVC) have lower friction than galvanized steel; this matters for long runs.

---

## Common Sizing Mistakes

- **Undersizing the main supply line** while correctly sizing branch lines — the main line must carry the sum of simultaneous branch flows.
- **Using nominal pipe size as inner diameter** — a 1″ copper Type L pipe has an inner diameter of ~25.4 mm, not 25.4 mm nominal. Differences can be 10–20% in cross-sectional area.
- **Ignoring velocity in hot water pipes** — using the same 2 m/s limit as cold water accelerates internal erosion, particularly in copper above 60 °C.
- **Forgetting equivalent pipe length for fittings** — a standard 90° elbow adds roughly 30–50× its diameter in equivalent straight pipe resistance.

---

## When to Consult a Licensed Plumber or Engineer

This calculator is appropriate for **preliminary sizing and educational purposes**. For new construction, renovations involving mains connections, or any system where inadequate pressure or flow poses a health or safety risk (hospitals, fire suppression, multi-story buildings), sizing must be validated by a qualified professional against local building codes.

faq.q: What is the formula to calculate pipe diameter from flow rate?
faq.a: Use **D = √(4Q / πV)**, where Q is flow rate in m³/s and V is velocity in m/s. For example, 1 L/s (0.001 m³/s) at 1.5 m/s gives D = √(4 × 0.001 / π × 1.5) = 0.0291 m = 29 mm inner diameter.

faq.q: What velocity should I use for residential water pipes?
faq.a: Most residential plumbing codes recommend **1.0–2.0 m/s** for cold water and **0.5–1.5 m/s** for hot water. This calculator uses 1.5 m/s as the default — a good balance that prevents water hammer and excessive pressure drop.

faq.q: What pipe diameter do I need for 1 L/s?
faq.a: At 1.5 m/s: minimum inner diameter = 29 mm. Use a **32 mm** standard commercial pipe. At 1.0 m/s: minimum is 36 mm, so use **40 mm** pipe. Higher velocity allows a smaller pipe but increases noise.

faq.q: What pipe size do I need for a house main supply line?
faq.a: A typical single-family home with simultaneous demand of 0.5–1.5 L/s should use **25–40 mm** inner diameter for the main supply line. Larger homes or those with pressure boosters may need 50–63 mm.

faq.q: How does flow rate relate to pipe diameter?
faq.a: Flow rate = velocity × cross-sectional area. Doubling the pipe diameter increases the area by 4×, so you can carry 4 times the flow at the same velocity. This is why going from 25 mm to 50 mm pipe makes a huge difference in capacity.

faq.q: What are standard commercial pipe sizes?
faq.a: Common nominal inner diameters for plastic and copper pipes are: **13, 20, 25, 32, 40, 50, 63, 75, 90, and 110 mm**. These correspond roughly to ½", ¾", 1", 1¼", 1½", 2", 2½", 3", 3½", and 4" nominal pipe size.

faq.q: Why is velocity 1.5 m/s the standard recommendation?
faq.a: Below 0.5 m/s, sediment can settle and biofilm grows. Above 2.5 m/s, pressure drops become excessive and pipes erode faster (especially copper). The 1.0–2.0 m/s range (1.5 m/s default) balances cost, noise, and longevity for most residential applications.

faq.q: How do I convert gallons per minute (GPM) to L/s?
faq.a: Multiply GPM by 0.0631 to get L/s. For example: 10 GPM × 0.0631 = 0.631 L/s. Then enter that value into this calculator to find the pipe diameter.

faq.q: Does pipe diameter affect water pressure?
faq.a: Yes. A smaller pipe increases flow velocity, which increases friction losses and reduces pressure at the outlet (Bernoulli's principle). For long pipe runs, always check that pressure at the end of the run meets minimum fixture requirements (typically 10–25 PSI / 0.7–1.7 bar for residential).
